doc.title: Hank Cicalo interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 30, 2022

title: Cannonball Adderley sessions and jazz studio workflow
summary: Hank says Cannonball and Nat Adderley were not isolated, and describes jazz groups working out tunes and complaining about phones.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Cannonball Adderley: the sound, the man, the band

blocks.x: I told you that I am a huge fan of Cannonball Adderley. I wondered, when you recorded them did Cannonball and Nat have to be in a separate booth?
You just had the band playing?

No. Everybody out there, everybody facing each other, everybody having contact. That was my thing always, to make the artist comfortable. If the artist wanted to sit with the drummer I’d put her out there with the drummer. You know? That’s his problem, not mine at that point. You know? I mean you’d get into the things, “I want to sit by the piano player because he can’t keep himself in time” or something.

I see. But generally speaking the jazz records, the jazz recordings took less time and I’m wondering, with Cannonball, would they play a tune and finish it and then come into the booth and like check it out, then say okay?

No. Everybody’s always checking it out. I mean right? In the studio they might work if you’ve got a group, and they might work on a tune for 15, 20 minutes. And you get your thing together in 20 minutes. I mean the guys out there, they’re not really interested in what you’re doing other than the fact that they want their phones to sound right. So really immediately when you’re starting a date immediately you’ve got to make the phones

right. They haven’t played two bars yet and they’re complaining about the phones. I would say, take the phones off, you know, let me get a balance and then we’ll go for it — and then you can ask more bass, more this more that. At least you get an engineer — I’ve never had trouble with the players. I know engineers have trouble with players. My feeling about rhythm sections was always not to put them all in booths all over the room but to put them together in a room so they’re all facing each other. So if it’s a guitar that’s really loud you can put him in a booth as long as he’s hearing it in his phone, and that makes it better for you to control it and it makes them comfortable so that they’re not overriding each other. And you could talk to them, I mean you know these guys, you could say, “Hey Jim, turn it down a little bit.” Or “Billy, the bass amplifier is too loud either turn it down or turn it away” we’ll work it out. You’ve got to make them comfortable. If the artists are comfortable your job is so much easier.
